ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Ethics: The Ethics Committee of UNISINOS approved the study (protocol number: 88282925.5.0000.5344), and all participants provided informed consent before participating.
A total of 124 participants completed the research procedure.

Participants were aged between 18 and 30 years, had no history of mental disorders affecting the dopaminergic system (e.g., schizophrenia), and were not taking medications known to influence this system (e.g., mood stabilizers or stimulants).
Participants first provided informed consent, completed a sociodemographic questionnaire, underwent the RL experimental task, and then completed the remaining self-report measures.
Participants were recruited via convenience sampling using social media platforms.

Initially, participants are instructed to learn, by trial and error, which of three buttons ("C", "B", or "M" on the computer keyboard) they should press when exposed to a specific stimulus on the screen.
Subsequently, participants are instructed to use the correct and incorrect feedback, after each attempt, to guide subsequent responses.
Participants were not instructed about this structure.
Participants were between 18 and 30 years old (M= 23.23; SD=2.62) and were mostly female (62.72%).

The majority of participants were undergraduate students (78.18%), white (89.09%), considered themselves cisgender, and had an average family income between R$ 7,600 and R$ 23,800 (42.72%), which corresponds to class C to B (middle to upper-middle class) in a commonly used Brazilian socioeconomic stratification.
First, the sample was composed exclusively of convenience participants recruited via social media, with limited demographic diversity.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. text.text: Reinforcement Sensitivity Theory (RST) is an influential framework explaining individual differences in sensitivity to reward and punishment.
The theory's empirical definitions require that self-report and behavioral measures of Reinforcement Learning (RL) correlate.
Recent experimental research has shown that RL is influenced by working memory (WM) load, challenging RST assumptions.

The aim of this pre-registered study was to evaluate the relationship between self-report RST measures and performance on an experimental RL task that isolates operant conditioning from the impact of WM.
A sample of 110 participants (aged 18-30) completed the RST-PQ, the BIS/BAS Scale, the Barratt Impulsiveness Scale (BIS-11), and the DASS-21.
In the laboratory, they responded to the computerized Reinforcement Learning/Working Memory (RLWM).

Behavioral performance was analyzed through Pearson/Spearman correlations, mediation analyses, and three computational models (Classic RL, RLWMi, and RLWMi + Deduction) were fitted to the data to estimate latent learning parameters.

Only the Fun Seeking subscale of the BIS/BAS Scale predicted learning, both in the behavioral measure under WM-controlled conditions (β= .190, p = .033) and, with greater magnitude, in the computationally modeled learning-rate parameter (β= .233, p = .020), derived from the best-fitting model (RLWMi + Deduction; AIC = 634.151).
Contrary to expectations, WM did not mediate this relationship in either condition.

Complementary analyses revealed that Behavioral Approach System (BAS) subfactors differentially correlate with distinct processes: while Fun Seeking predicted the positive reinforcement parameter but not perseverative errors, Reward Reactivity predicted perseverative errors but not learning rate, and Reward Interest showed marginal associations with both.

These results suggest that different personality traits map onto distinct computational mechanisms of reward-and punishment-based learning, independently of WM, and that computational modeling detects these associations with greater sensitivity than raw behavioral performance.
The ability to learn from rewards and punishments is fundamental for adaptive behavior across all species and varies between individuals (Donahoe, 2017).
text.formatted: The ability to learn from rewards and punishments is fundamental for adaptive behavior across all species and varies between individuals <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Donahoe, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Understanding why individuals differ in the way they learn remains a central challenge in psychology, cognitive neuroscience, and psychopathology research (McNaughton, 2025).
text.formatted: Understanding why individuals differ in the way they learn remains a central challenge in psychology, cognitive neuroscience, and psychopathology research <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(McNaughton, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Some researchers rely on personality theories to answer why individual differences in learning mechanisms exist. Pavlov (1927) proposed that personality/temperament may reflect the sensitivity from the nervous system to excite or inhibit responses from stimuli.
text.formatted: Some researchers rely on personality theories to answer why individual differences in learning mechanisms exist. <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Pavlov (1927)</ref> proposed that personality/temperament may reflect the sensitivity from the nervous system to excite or inhibit responses from stimuli.

text.text: His work inspired Gray's theory of personality, which proposes that biologically grounded motivational systems regulate sensitivity to appetitive and aversive stimulation.
Gray proposed the Reinforcement Sensitivity Theory (RST) to explain individual differences in sensitivity to reward and punishment (Gray, 1982; Gray & McNaughton, 2000).
text.formatted: Gray proposed the Reinforcement Sensitivity Theory (RST) to explain individual differences in sensitivity to reward and punishment <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Gray, 1982;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Gray & McNaughton, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: The theory relies on two constructs to capture reinforcement sensitivity, i.e., how organisms react to internal or environmental cues while learning by conditioning processes.
The first construct is sensitivity to reward, which represents how the presentation of appetitive stimuli or removal of aversive stimuli change behavior.
The second construct is sensitivity to punishment, which represents how the presentation of aversive stimuli or removal of appetitive stimuli influences negative reinforcement.

While sensitivity to reward is related to a myriad of brain areas titled the Behavioral Approach System (BAS), sensitivity to punishment is related to two systems, the Behavioral Inhibition System (BIS) and the Fight-Flight-Freeze system (FFFS) (Gray & McNaughton, 2000).
text.formatted: While sensitivity to reward is related to a myriad of brain areas titled the Behavioral Approach System (BAS), sensitivity to punishment is related to two systems, the Behavioral Inhibition System (BIS) and the Fight-Flight-Freeze system (FFFS) <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Gray & McNaughton, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: In an effort to translate the neuroanatomical systems (BAS, BIS and FFFS) from theory into observable measures, a series of self-report measures were developed taking into account the assumptions of RST (Carver & White, 1994; Corr, 2016).
text.formatted: In an effort to translate the neuroanatomical systems (BAS, BIS and FFFS) from theory into observable measures, a series of self-report measures were developed taking into account the assumptions of RST <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Carver & White, 1994;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Corr, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: These instruments differ into theoretical assumptions, such as a uni/multidimensional scales to measure BAS reactivity, homogeneity or even heterogeneity between BIS and FFFS measures, and validation process.

Meanwhile, most of the questionnaires rely on the theory assumption of reactivity over description, uncommon in other personality measures; The items asks how individuals react over an approachable or aversive context (Corr, 2016).
text.formatted: Meanwhile, most of the questionnaires rely on the theory assumption of reactivity over description, uncommon in other personality measures; The items asks how individuals react over an approachable or aversive context <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Corr, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Given its neurobiological roots, a central assumption of the theory is the need for its questionnaires to correlate with behavioral performance in conditioning procedures.
Overall, few of its measures have undergone the behavioral validation assumed by the theory.
Meta-analytic data obtained with old RST measures or adapted personality questionnaires provided insights into the relationship between RST measures and reinforcement (Leue & Beauducel, 2008).
text.formatted: Meta-analytic data obtained with old RST measures or adapted personality questionnaires provided insights into the relationship between RST measures and reinforcement <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Leue & Beauducel, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: A relationship between anxiety and impulsivity traits with conditioning procedures was observed using experimental tasks, however, there is a lack of consistency between different questionnaires and experimental procedures, with too much heterogeneity in effect sizes.
Indirect tests of the association between personality and reinforcement performance have been made, mostly with clinical groups.
For instance, sex offenders show heightened reward sensitivity and less adaptive behavior in conflict situations when compared to non-offenders (Leue et al., 2008).
text.formatted: For instance, sex offenders show heightened reward sensitivity and less adaptive behavior in conflict situations when compared to non-offenders <ref type="bibr">(Leue et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: In another example, RST self-report measures effectively clustered acute pain responsiveness by categorizing individuals into "pain avoiders", with high BIS, flight/freezing traits and greater pain sensitivity, and "pain approachers," who exhibit high BAS, fight traits, and lower overall pain sensitivity (Vetterlein et al., 2024).
text.formatted: In another example, RST self-report measures effectively clustered acute pain responsiveness by categorizing individuals into "pain avoiders", with high BIS, flight/freezing traits and greater pain sensitivity, and "pain approachers," who exhibit high BAS, fight traits, and lower overall pain sensitivity <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Vetterlein et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The literature about Reinforcement Learning (RL) has grown exponentially over the past few years.
This is due to computational modeling of (RL) procedures in computational neuroscience studies.

It is already known that RL depends on dopamine and its tonic and phasic functioning in the corticobasal ganglion-thalamo-cortical (CBGTC) circuit, composed of a set of neuroanatomical areas that regulate the orientation of behaviors to acquire rewards and avoid punishments.

Knowledge of a specific circuit has allowed the advancement of RL studies through mathematical models and algorithms that "simulate" the functioning of the CBGTC network and dopaminergic action with computational tests (Maia & Frank, 2011).
text.formatted: Knowledge of a specific circuit has allowed the advancement of RL studies through mathematical models and algorithms that "simulate" the functioning of the CBGTC network and dopaminergic action with computational tests <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Maia & Frank, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: The advantage of computational analyses lies in the hypothesis testing they allow: It is not possible to observe the CBGTC system functioning in vivo, even with current neuroimaging technologies.

Therefore, by using algorithms that aim to capture the RL process, computational analyses allow for hypothesis testing that simulates brain function moment by moment as an individual learns (Wilson & Collins, 2019).
text.formatted: Therefore, by using algorithms that aim to capture the RL process, computational analyses allow for hypothesis testing that simulates brain function moment by moment as an individual learns <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Wilson & Collins, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Another advantage of using computational analysis is its use in attempting to explain the relationship between different cognitive and behavioral processes, as is the case with the relationship between RL and Working Memory (WM) that was distinguished in previous studies (Collins, 2018; Weydmann et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Another advantage of using computational analysis is its use in attempting to explain the relationship between different cognitive and behavioral processes, as is the case with the relationship between RL and Working Memory (WM) that was distinguished in previous studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Collins, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Weydmann et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: WM is a cognitive process that enables the temporary storage and manipulation of information necessary for complex tasks.
It is essential for maintaining and processing information in short periods, which allows for tasks such as problem-solving, calculations, and planning (Barak & Tsodyks, 2014).
text.formatted: It is essential for maintaining and processing information in short periods, which allows for tasks such as problem-solving, calculations, and planning <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Barak & Tsodyks, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Although cognitive psychology assumed that RL and WM acted independently, competing only for the decision of action, recent evidence suggests that WM can interfere with RL calculations, mainly in reward prediction errors, which are crucial for the individual to be able to update the expected value in an RA relationship (Collins et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Although cognitive psychology assumed that RL and WM acted independently, competing only for the decision of action, recent evidence suggests that WM can interfere with RL calculations, mainly in reward prediction errors, which are crucial for the individual to be able to update the expected value in an RA relationship <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Collins et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: However, even with exponential advances in the areas of RL and RST in the last decade, the question regarding their relationship between personality and reinforcement performance has been almost silenced, even though today there are theoretical and methodological advances that can answer this question with greater precision.

Therefore, the present study aims to evaluate the relationship between different self-report measures of RST and performance on an experimental reinforcement task that isolates operant conditioning by controlling the impact of WM on learning processes.
The current study and its hypothesis were pre-registered at Open Science Framework at Marques et al. (2025) (https://osf.io/qh4c6).
text.formatted: The current study and its hypothesis were pre-registered at Open Science Framework at <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Marques et al. (2025)</ref> (<ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/qh4c6">https://osf.io/qh4c6</ref>).

text.text: We hypothesized that learning rate, as assessed by the percentage of correct responses and computationally modeled, would correlate with some of the RST factors when WM is not demanded.
In short, the correlations between the RST and Reinforcement Learning depend on the WM.
A total of 124 participants completed the research procedure.
After applying the exclusion criteria, a total of 110 were kept for final analysis after removing 14 individuals who scored below the 75% cut-off score on the experimental task.

Participants were aged between 18 and 30 years, had no history of mental disorders affecting the dopaminergic system (e.g., schizophrenia), and were not taking medications known to influence this system (e.g., mood stabilizers or stimulants).
Participants first provided informed consent, completed a sociodemographic questionnaire, underwent the RL experimental task, and then completed the remaining self-report measures.
Participants were recruited via convenience sampling using social media platforms.
The RST-PQ is a self-report scale based on the theoretical assumptions of the revised version of Reinforcement Sensitivity Theory (rRST).

Developed by Corr & Cooper (2016) and currently being adapted, the measure consists of 65 items corresponding to the neuroanatomical systems of reward (Behavioral Approach System, acronym BAS) and punishment sensitivity (Behavioral Inhibition System, acronym BIS; Fight-Flight-Freeze System, acronym FFFS).

text.text: The respondent must analyze each item considering their own behavior and rate them according to a 4-point Likert scale:1 = rarely or never;2 = occasionally;3 = frequently;4 = almost always/always.
The scale score ranges from 30 to 120 points, and high scores indicate the presence of impulsive behaviors.

text.text: This task was adapted from Collins (2018) and assesses how WM overload affects RL performance.
text.formatted: This task was adapted from <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Collins (2018)</ref> and assesses how WM overload affects RL performance.

text.text: Initially, participants are instructed to learn, by trial and error, which of three buttons ("C", "B", or "M" on the computer keyboard) they should press when exposed to a specific stimulus on the screen.
Subsequently, participants are instructed to use the correct and incorrect feedback, after each attempt, to guide subsequent responses.
Feedback is presented following a continuous reinforcement schedule.
Thus, the task contains 14 blocks and manipulates memory under different conditions, with low (8 blocks) or high (6 blocks) WM load conditions.
In the low WM load condition, three stimuli are presented in pseudo-random order, while in the high WM load condition, six stimuli are presented.
In each block, the discriminative visual condition of the stimuli (i.e., color, geometric figures, drawing, etc.) is altered to ensure that the participant engages in a new learning process.
All stimuli are presented nine times, totaling 540 trials.
Each trial consisted of a cross-fixation (500 ms), followed by a visual stimulus presented until participants responded, and then a feedback screen for 1000 ms (displaying "correct" or "incorrect").
Participants performed 24 training trials using six stimuli unrelated to the main task before the final evaluation (Figure 1).
text.formatted: Participants performed 24 training trials using six stimuli unrelated to the main task before the final evaluation (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: From the RLWM outcomes, we extracted 2-Back and 3-Back scores to represent WM, as well as four learning scores that control for WM use: two related to learning by positive reinforcement (with and without cognitive overload) and two related to perseverative errors in both conditions.

Furthermore, this version of the task allowed the participant to use deductive reasoning in learning by relating a letter to a stimulus in low-overload condition, and a letter to two stimuli in high-overload condition (Weydmann et al., 2025).

text.text: This model has eight parameters, including Learning Rate (α), beta (β), decay (φ), which indicates the effects of forgetting correct responses between trials, Persistence (pers), which controls the effects of neglecting negative feedback and making repeated errors for the same stimulus; and Random Noise (ε), which captures lapses in action of random responses.
The Response Bias (init) model captures biases in how participants initiate their responses in each block; η3 and η6 were created to simulate WM use under low (η3) and high (η6) WM load.
Finally, the last model tested was RLWMi + Deduction (Weydmann et al., 2025), which assumes that some participants used deduction to solve the task and others did not.
text.formatted: Finally, the last model tested was RLWMi + Deduction <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Weydmann et al., 2025)</ref>, which assumes that some participants used deduction to solve the task and others did not.

text.text: Here, deduction represents participants' attempt to "guess" the correct answer based on previous correct answers.
This model includes all the parameters previously mentioned in RLWMi and adds two more related to deduction: gamma (γ) RL and γ WM.
These parameters were used to estimate how much deduction influenced the effects of RL or WM, respectively.
Our statistical procedure aligns with our hypotheses, and tests were performed in RStudio (R Core Team, 2024).
We initially developed five hypotheses for this study.
The exploratory hypotheses initially propose that Pearson' correlations between RST personality factors and RLWM performance will not be statistically significant (H0).

However, we expected RST personality factors to show significant correlations with experimental outcomes, while self-report scores from instruments not linked to RST (DASS-21 and BIS-11) would not correlate significantly with RLWM scores (H1).

Specifically, we expected correlations between RST scores and the following learning scores: The percentage of accuracy under low cognitive load (PCorrect3) and high cognitive load (PCorrect6), and the computational parameter Learning rate (α).

Our main hypotheses predict that a) the personality factor with the highest correlation with learning under low cognitive load will have its effect mediated by the use of WM (H2), while RST factors associated with learning under high cognitive load will not have their correlation mediated by WM (H3).
To test these hypotheses, mediation analyses were conducted, with WM represented by the N-back score most strongly correlated with the accuracy outcomes (PCorrect3 and Pcorrect6).
Following the use of computational analyses, the personality factor selected by the exploratory tests conducted after H1 and H2 was expected to correlate with the α parameter.
If significant, this correlation was expected to be mediated by the computational parameter η₃ (H4).
On the other hand, it is also predicted that if personality correlates significantly with α, the association would not be mediated by the η₆ parameter (H5).
Mediation analyses were conducted in R using the lavaan package (Version 0.6-21; Rosseel, 2012; Rosseel et al., 2025).

text.text: This study aimed to clarify the relationship between personality and behavior.
Based on RST, we tested how personality factors correlate with RL processes at distinct phases of WM load.
Some of our hypotheses were confirmed: RST personality factors were associated with RL performance regardless of WM use.
Nonetheless, our hypotheses regarding the mediation effects of WM were not confirmed.
Furthermore, self-report measures unrelated to RST (BIS-11 and DASS-21 scores) were not associated with learning measures, as hypothesized.

The finding that only the Fun Seeking subscale of the BIS/BAS Scales correlated with learning, in both behavioral and modeled measures, deserves careful interpretation, particularly given existing psychometric criticisms of this factor. Krupić et al. (2016) demonstrated that Fun Seeking was the only BAS subscale that failed to fit adequately in a convergent validity model comparing five RST questionnaires Fun seeking also presented reliability coefficients below the commonly accepted threshold of .70.

(2016)</ref> demonstrated that Fun Seeking was the only BAS subscale that failed to fit adequately in a convergent validity model comparing five RST questionnaires Fun seeking also presented reliability coefficients below the commonly accepted threshold of .70.

text.text: Additionally, Fun Seeking has been identified as the only BAS subscale that overlaps with impulsivity measures (Alloy et al., 2009), and previous research has argued that existing BAS measures conflate reward sensitivity with rash impulsivity, two processes that revised RST attempts to separate (Smillie et al., 2006).

text.text: From a theoretical standpoint, this overlap between Fun Seeking and impulsivity may actually explain why this factor, rather than other BAS dimensions, correlated with learning rate.

Fun Seeking was designed to capture hedonic reward sensitivity and spontaneous approach toward immediately rewarding stimuli (Carver & White, 1994), which maps more directly onto the dopaminergic RL processes and model-free behavior indexed by the learning parameter in the CBGTC circuit.
text.formatted: Fun Seeking was designed to capture hedonic reward sensitivity and spontaneous approach toward immediately rewarding stimuli <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Carver & White, 1994)</ref>, which maps more directly onto the dopaminergic RL processes and model-free behavior indexed by the learning parameter in the CBGTC circuit.

text.text: In contrast, factors such as Goal-Drive Persistence and Drive involve planning and goal-directed behavior that rely more heavily on executive control and model-based processes.

As shown in previous studies (De Pascalis et al., 2018), some BAS factors may relate to higher-order cognitive processes which rely more heavily on prefrontal executive functions and WM than on phasic dopaminergic signaling.
text.formatted: As shown in previous studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(De Pascalis et al., 2018)</ref>, some BAS factors may relate to higher-order cognitive processes which rely more heavily on prefrontal executive functions and WM than on phasic dopaminergic signaling.

text.text: These associations with higher-order cognition may dilute their association with pure operant/model-free conditioning as measured in the RLWM task.
Beyond observable behavioral measures, computational modeling provided a methodological advantage in detecting the relationship between personality and RL in the present study.

The effect size of the association between Fun Seeking and the learning rate parameter was greater in the computational analysis (β = .233, p = .020) than in the behavioral measure (β = .190, p = .033), suggesting that computational modeling captures individual differences in RL with greater sensitivity than raw performance scores.

This finding aligns with the broader argument that computational models, by simulating the trial-by-trial computations underlying behavior, isolate latent variables that are not directly observable in aggregate performance measures (Kriegeskorte & Douglas, 2018).
text.formatted: This finding aligns with the broader argument that computational models, by simulating the trial-by-trial computations underlying behavior, isolate latent variables that are not directly observable in aggregate performance measures <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Kriegeskorte & Douglas, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Specifically, the learning rate parameter reflects the degree to which reward prediction errors update expected values in the CBGTC circuit on each trial; a process that is mathematically distinct from overall accuracy, which is also influenced by WM use, deductive reasoning, and response noise (Weydmann et al., 2025).

text.text: The distinction between behavioral mechanisms is theoretically important.
Previous studies have shown that aggregate RL performance scores conflate multiple behavioral mechanisms that can be dissociated computationally.

For instance, Weydmann et al. (2025) demonstrated that decreased RL performance in individuals with elevated Body Mass Index (BMI) were better explained by persistence and deduction computational parameters rather than WM use.
text.formatted: For instance, <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Weydmann et al. (2025)</ref> demonstrated that decreased RL performance in individuals with elevated Body Mass Index (BMI) were better explained by persistence and deduction computational parameters rather than WM use.

text.text: Similarly, the present data suggest that the relationship between Fun Seeking and learning may have been attenuated in behavioral measures by WM and other executive functions operating simultaneously during task performance.
By isolating RL with the learning rate parameter, the computational analysis provided a cleaner estimate of the reinforcement signal that personality traits are theoretically proposed to modulate.

These results support the recommendation that future studies investigating RST and RL adopt computational modeling as a primary analytical tool, rather than relying exclusively on behavioral performance scores.
An exploratory and theoretically informative finding concerns the differential associations between BAS subfactors and distinct RL processes.
These results suggest that BAS subfactors do not uniformly map onto RL processes, but rather dissociate depending if positive or negative reinforcement are controlling behavior.
This dissociation is consistent with the neurobiological architecture of the CBGTC circuit, where positive and negative reinforcement are regulated by distinct dopaminergic mechanisms.

Phasic dopamine bursts following unexpected rewards drive D1 receptor-mediated GO signals that strengthen approach behavior, while tonic dopamine depletion following negative outcomes drives D2 receptor-mediated stop signals that promote avoidance and behavioral flexibility (Maia & Frank, 2011).
text.formatted: Phasic dopamine bursts following unexpected rewards drive D1 receptor-mediated GO signals that strengthen approach behavior, while tonic dopamine depletion following negative outcomes drives D2 receptor-mediated stop signals that promote avoidance and behavioral flexibility <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Maia & Frank, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: From this perspective, Fun Seeking with its emphasis on hedonic reactivity and spontaneous approach toward immediately rewarding stimuli may be more closely aligned with the phasic dopaminergic signaling underlying positive reinforcement.

Reward Reactivity, however, captures the emotional response of receiving a reward, and its association with perseverative errors may reflect a tendency to change approach behavior in the face of negative feedback.

Taken together, these findings highlight that the BAS is not a unitary construct with respect to RL, and that its subfactors may selectively modulate distinct computational parameters within the RL framework.

Future studies should systematically investigate these differential associations, ideally combining RST measures with computational modeling to map personality traits onto specific components of the dopaminergic learning system.
Several limitations of the present study warrant acknowledgment.
First, the sample was composed exclusively of convenience participants recruited via social media, with limited demographic diversity.

This homogeneity restricts the generalizability of the findings to broader populations, and the predominance of female participants (62.72%) may have introduced systematic variance given evidence that sex influences RST trait expression, RL conditioning patterns, and frontal asymmetry patterns associated with BAS (Evans & Hampson, 2015; De Pascalis et al., 2018).
text.formatted: This homogeneity restricts the generalizability of the findings to broader populations, and the predominance of female participants (62.72%) may have introduced systematic variance given evidence that sex influences RST trait expression, RL conditioning patterns, and frontal asymmetry patterns associated with BAS <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Evans & Hampson, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">De Pascalis et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Future studies should prioritize more demographically diverse samples or clinical samples to broaden the understanding of personality and learning.

Furthermore, although adequate for the primary correlational analyses, the sample size may have been insufficient to detect smaller magnitude effects, as suggested by the marginal association between Reward Interest and learning rate (p = .066).
Statistical power limitations are particularly relevant in computational modeling, where parameter estimation is sensitive to individual variability and the number of free parameters in the model.
Finally, other measures that impact the RL task such as intelligence, sleep patterns and substance use, were not controlled since they were unrelated to our main hypotheses.
The present findings open several promising avenues for future research at the intersection of personality neuroscience, computational psychiatry, and RL.

To our knowledge, this is the first study to directly test the association between RST factors and RL while controlling for different executive mechanisms both at the behavioral and computational level.

Also, the present paradigm could be extended to clinical populations where RST traits and RL are known to be disrupted, such as substance use disorders, attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder, and mood disorders (Maia & Frank, 2011; Katz et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Also, the present paradigm could be extended to clinical populations where RST traits and RL are known to be disrupted, such as substance use disorders, attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder, and mood disorders <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Maia & Frank, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Katz et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: In these contexts, isolating RL parameters from WM contributions may help disentangle whether clinical impairments reflect deficits in reward sensitivity, punishment sensitivity, deductive reasoning, or WM per se, with direct implications for intervention design.

Finally, the marginal association observed for Reward Interest warrants replication in larger samples, as this subfactor may represent a theoretically meaningful link between stimuli salience and reinforcement learning that the current study lacked statistical power to confirm.

Together, these directions suggest that combining revised RST frameworks, computational modeling, and neuropsychological assessment offers a productive path toward a more psychobiologically grounded understanding of how personality shapes interactions with life events.
